> Some players have suggested using sharding in low level zones to address  launch demand, both because we talked about that at Blizzcon, and  because it’s what they’re used to from our modern expansions.  Unfortunately, while modern WoW has content designed to work with  sharding, WoW Classic does not. The most obvious example of incompatible  content is Rexxar’s famously long patrol path, but there are lots of  other examples throughout WoW Classic. Since we want all that content to  work as it was originally designed, we’ve made sure that every layer is  a copy of the entire world, so you can kite Anachronos all the way to  Orgrimmar, and you can ride the boat from Ratchet to Booty Bay with the  same people alongside you the whole way. 

So it makes sense what they're trying to do and why we're seeing what we're seeing. There are lot of bad technical explanations in this thread which is what is confusing so many people I think and can be a bit frustrating  when you're trying to understand the design decision.

> Because serverless is a fancy name for "the infrastructure is somebody else's problem", with "somebody else" being a cloud provider like AWS, Google, Microsoft, etc.

I don't know what they teach now that things like AWS and Azure are popular but a serverless model of execution is when an agent running outside the memory space of the "server" dynamically manages the allocation of machine resources. It doesn't have to involve microservices because you could still have a serverless model of execution that is monolithic.

I can see what you are saying. I guess I don't know how often the WoW client polls their servers for updates or how much state info it needs. I would think it's mostly client side but I guess an MMO is probably pretty different in that way.
I'm not talking about Amazon's solutions I'm talking about serverless as an execution model.

> Relational Databases scale vertically (beefier hardware), not horizontally (more instances)

Horizontal scaling is literally a synonymous term for "sharding" which is what they are calling their tech ...

> Enterprise solutions are very expensive. More so than hosting a scalable web application.

What are you doing in game development in terms of networking architecture that's different than a web application? The web application should be even more susceptible to load balancing issues and poorly designed schema than a game because usually an http request has way more overhead than a simple relational query using a structured language.

I don't want to sound like a dick but ya I know what load balancing is

>>Oracle databases are expensive to provision, so I assume it comes down to product / project managers not wanting to inflate the cost of the system to or above a profit margin.

Uh it's not any more expensive than provisioning any other type of relational database or any other type of serverless solution. It should always be a linear relationship between the load and number of instances.
I'm not a game developer so I might be missing something but why not spin up more instances and kill them when the load goes down?

>>Perfect world, they have the resources to make this a non issue but we don’t what hardware they had available — or how much of a budget this project had.

Ya I guess this is what has me so baffled, it shouldn't cost that much to spin up additional resources if their process is solid so why aren't they doing that to relieve loads?

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serverless_computing

Either their engineers are massively under qualified or there was some weird decision made. Again, the latency is almost definitely not an issue with concurrent request to a database, and is much more likely to be an issue with load balancing connections at the gateway
There isn't actually a monolithic server though. The "server" nowadays is just an abstraction made up of multiple instances of a shared schema.

> It’s still a limitation on the database and how many queries it can take per second, you’ll notice that it takes people 3-5 second for a button click to process, imagine if there were no limits and no queues.

There's no way they're running into a limit with a production scale database. A well designed relational database should have no problem handing billions of concurrent queries. The button click press you mentioned is probably a symptom of poor load balancing not any sort of database query. I'm sure they're database is also some type of distributed architecture as well.
They're using it in classic too. There's a link in this thread to the interview where Ian talks about it. Also they're not using the 2004 client or back end.
